interviewQuestions.question: Why do CPUs use L1/L2/L3 instead of just one bigger, well-tuned cache?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Access latency grows with cache size because bigger SRAM arrays need longer wires and more time to search their tags — you can't make a structure both big enough for a modern working set and fast enough to answer in one or two cycles; those two goals pull in opposite directions on the same silicon.

So the hierarchy stacks several sizes instead of picking one: L1 stays tiny (32-64 KB, 1-4 cycles) so it can be searched fast enough to keep up with the pipeline's issue rate. L2 (256 KB-2 MB, ~10 cycles) catches what L1 evicts, still fast enough to be much cheaper than going further. L3 (tens of MB, shared across cores, ~30-50 cycles) catches what L2 can't hold, still dramatically cheaper than the ~100-300+ cycles a trip to DRAM costs. Each level trades size for speed at a different point on the curve, and most accesses get resolved by whichever level is cheapest for that particular piece of data's reuse pattern.

The number that ties it together is AMAT: a single big cache tuned to "good enough" latency for its size would have a *worse* average access time than a hierarchy, because most accesses (which hit in L1 in a well-behaved program) would pay that single cache's slower latency on every access instead of L1's near-instant one. The hierarchy lets the common case (hits in the smallest level) stay fast while still providing capacity for the less common case.

**Testing:** whether you see this as a physical size-vs-latency constraint that a single cache size can't escape, not an arbitrary design choice.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why the hierarchy has levels

interviewQuestions.question: What's the difference between an inclusive and an exclusive cache hierarchy, and why would you choose one?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Inclusive means every line in L1 is guaranteed to also exist in L2 (and L2's contents in L3, if there's a third level) — L2 is a strict superset of L1's contents. Exclusive means a line lives in exactly one level at a time; when it's promoted to L1 it's removed from L2, and evicting it from L1 sends it back down to L2 rather than discarding it.

Inclusive hierarchies make cross-core coherence simpler and cheaper at scale: a coherence check against the shared L3 (which, if inclusive down to L1, is guaranteed to know about every line any core's L1/L2 might have) can answer "does anyone have this line" without having to snoop every core's private caches individually — this is a big reason inclusive L3s were common in multi-socket Intel designs. The cost is wasted capacity: every byte cached in L1 is *also* consuming space in L2 and L3, so the effective usable capacity of the hierarchy is less than the sum of the levels' sizes.

Exclusive hierarchies use the full combined capacity — a line only occupies space once across all levels — at the cost of needing an explicit protocol to keep coherence information correct without relying on "the last level knows everything," and needing a separate copy-on-evict step (moving a line down rather than just discarding it) to maintain exclusivity, which adds bus traffic between levels. AMD's Zen-line L3 designs, for example, have historically leaned more exclusive/mostly-exclusive to maximize usable capacity, while some Intel designs favored inclusive L3 for the coherence simplification. There isn't a universally correct answer — it's a real trade-off between usable capacity and coherence-check simplicity that different vendors have made differently across generations.

**Testing:** whether you can name the actual trade-off (capacity vs coherence-check simplicity) rather than just defining the two terms.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Inclusive vs exclusive hierarchies

interviewQuestions.question: You're profiling a multithreaded application and see high L3 miss rate but low L1/L2 miss rates per core. What does that combination suggest, and how would you investigate further?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Low per-core L1/L2 miss rates mean each thread's own working set fits comfortably in its private levels — so the L3 misses aren't coming from any single thread's data simply being "too big." High L3 miss rate despite that points toward one of a few specific causes rather than a generic "needs bigger cache" fix, and I'd investigate in that order.

First, aggregate footprint: L3 is shared across cores, so even if each core's *own* working set is small, N cores each touching a different large dataset can collectively exceed L3 capacity — the fix there is either genuinely more L3 (a hardware constraint you can't change at runtime) or reducing per-core footprint (streaming instead of caching everything, or partitioning work so cores share data rather than each touching a disjoint large set). Second, cross-core coherence traffic: if multiple cores are reading and invalidating the same lines (shared mutable state, or false sharing at a coarser granularity than L1 alone would show), that shows up as L3 misses/coherence traffic even though each core's local caches look fine in isolation — `perf c2c` or equivalent cross-core-communication profiling tools are built exactly for this. Third, prefetcher interaction: L3 often relies on different, more conservative prefetch logic than L1/L2, so an access pattern that L1/L2 prefetchers handle well can still generate genuine L3 misses if L3's prefetcher doesn't recognize the same stride pattern.

I'd pull per-core cache-miss counters alongside cross-core coherence-traffic counters before concluding it's a capacity problem — the symptom described is consistent with at least two very different root causes that need different fixes.

**Testing:** whether you can reason from a specific counter pattern to multiple plausible causes and know which tools distinguish them, rather than jumping straight to "add more L3."
